episode_summary: TBP83 (September 2016) explores the Lightning Network with guest Olaoluwa Osuntokun (Roast Beef), who covers the layered design, payment channels, onion-routed payments, the draft specification, his Go implementation and throughput tests, cross-chain use, and the time-lock and usability challenges. Steven Mackie (Yours) and Valerian Bennett (PopChest) describe how Lightning micropayments would fit their content platforms.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Olaoluwa Osuntokun said several teams were building Lightning, including Rusty and Christian Decker at Blockstream.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: There's several teams working on Lightning currently. There's Rusty and Christian Decker at Blockstream.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said the Lightning specification would probably have an initial V1 out pretty soon.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: And that's what we're doing on the specification realm. We'll probably have initial V1 out pretty soon.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said his Lightning implementation could open and close channels and send single-hop payments quickly.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: And where our implementation is currently is, you can open and close channels. You can do single-hot payments pretty quickly.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun reported a re-recorded Lightning demo between two DigitalOcean nodes that ran 1,000 HTLCs a second.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: I found it basically just a full blast test. I got to run 1,000 HTLCs a second,

cards.claim: Osuntokun explained that in Lightning's onion-routed payments each hop learns only the previous and next destination, not the source or final recipient.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: So each person within the route only learns basically the previous and the next destination, and they don't learn the source or the ultimate destination.

cards.claim: Osuntokun described Lightning as layered, with Bitcoin as the base layer and bidirectional payment channels as the second layer.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: Then the second layer is basically the payment channels, the bidirectional payment channels.

cards.claim: Osuntokun compared Lightning's bonded channels to proof-of-stake, where smart contracts make cheaters lose their funds.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: in this you have a similar bonding system and you set up a series of smart contracts such that you will lose your bond if you try to violate the contract.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said Lightning throughput could scale linearly with the number of nodes and channels.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: It can essentially scale linearly as the number of nodes and the number of increases.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun predicted that once the Lightning specification was published, any company or wallet provider could implement Lightning and a diverse network would follow.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: And once we get that out there, basically, anyone can implement Lightning. Any company, any wallet provider, and we'll have basically a pretty diverse network, I'm imagining.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun predicted Lightning would let altcoins such as Dogecoin and Litecoin trade by routing through Bitcoin.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: so i have like dogecoin on one side and light coin on the other side and we're trading we're actually going through bitcoin

cards.claim: Osuntokun said the main compatibility requirement for other blockchains to join Lightning is the same hash function as Bitcoin.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: the main compatibility layer is kind of in the smart contract system of the blockchains where we basically require one of two things.

cards.claim: Osuntokun said other blockchains joining Lightning would also need time locks such as CSV or CheckLockTimeVerify.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: And then also you need some sort of notion of time locks where you say I can't spend this Bitcoin until or whatever coin you have until either some block or some actual absolute time within the future.

cards.claim: Osuntokun described Lightning as a series of atomic swaps, with only the entry transaction made on-chain.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: Well, Lightning is basically a series of atomic swaps, but completely on-chain.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Valerian Bennett said user experience was an even bigger hurdle than the technology for PopChest's micropayments.
cards.speaker: Valerian Bennett
cards.quote: But an even bigger part, at least initially, is really just the user experience part of it.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Valerian Bennett said PopChest was a pay-per-view platform that would need to cut per-second costs to sub-penny levels for streaming and music.
cards.speaker: Valerian Bennett
cards.quote: So right now we're basically a pay-per-view system, but if we ever want to do streaming, if we ever want to do live streaming, if we ever want to do music

cards.claim: In September 2016 Stephen Mackie described Yours as a Reddit-like site where users submit links and content and micro-endorse posts with Lightning payments.
cards.speaker: Steven Mackie
cards.quote: So essentially what you do is you submit links and threads and content onto the site.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Stephen Mackie said Yours users would have complete control of their funds and could withdraw them at any time.
cards.speaker: Steven Mackie
cards.quote: And users have complete control of their funds at any time.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Stephen Mackie described Steemit as a platform for content creation and curation where rewards depended on existing steem power and reputation.
cards.speaker: Steven Mackie
cards.quote: trying to be like a platform for content creation and curation, right? More so at this point, it seems to be curation and people writing very interesting thought pieces.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said Lightning's pain points were both technical and in how the technology is presented to users.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: Yeah, so there are pain points in the technology itself, but then also the presentation to the user.

cards.claim: Osuntokun said that after a Lightning node failed, users might wait a day or two, or up to a week, to get their money back.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: you get your money back, but you may need to wait like a day or two or, you know, or like maybe up to a week.

cards.claim: Osuntokun proposed watchers, or outsourcers, who would claim a user's funds on their behalf if the user was offline.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: you can have basically something we'll call them like a watcher or like an outsourcer kind of help you out with that.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said the Bitcoin space lacked designers and UX engineers, and that wallets such as Electrum were rudimentary.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: We don't have as many like designers and, you know, UX engineers actually in the space.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said Lightning routing fees would be very low at first, perhaps zero, and rise as competition developed.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: we expect that fee to be very, very low initially just because, you know, maybe it'll be zero at first.

cards.claim: Osuntokun explained that Lightning uses a contestation period after an event, so a party can challenge an invalid action before the blockchain settles it.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: what Lightning does is when an event happens, there's kind of like a contestation period where you need to wait a certain amount of time

cards.claim: In September 2016 Stephen Mackie said channels needed someone online to close them once they had accumulated enough funds, a problem Yours wanted to solve.
cards.speaker: Steven Mackie
cards.quote: It's accumulated enough funds. Like someone needs to come online and say, hey, close this close, close this channel

cards.claim: In September 2016 an unnamed guest said the plan was technology people could use without knowing how the underlying system works.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: The plan is to create technology that people can use without having to know what they're doing.

cards.claim: In September 2016 Osuntokun said he hoped users would eventually just download a Lightning app on their phone, as with early browsers.
cards.speaker: Olaoluwa Osuntokun
cards.quote: hopefully we get to that point where it's just like, you know, download the app on your phone

cards.claim: In September 2016 Stephen Mackie said Yours users would not need to go through an exchange to get their money out.
cards.speaker: Steven Mackie
cards.quote: you don't have to go through an exchange to get your money out

cards.claim: In September 2016 an unnamed host said Bitcoin's technical innovation in cryptography came from problems Bitcoin itself offered to solve.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: A lot of the world's first so far in innovations in cryptography that no one has really given a lot of thought to have come to being because they needed to solve a problem that Bitcoin offered.

cards.claim: In September 2016 a host said academics were increasingly engaging with Bitcoin, with top conferences starting to accept papers on it.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: and then also increasingly more so now, academics are starting to become more involved in Bitcoin.

title: TBP83 - Lightning Network Deep Dive
